cards.text: This one's a letter from a man named James, to the twelve tribes of the Dispersion. His whole hello is one word: “Greetings.” That's ALL the small talk you're getting, friend.

cards.question: In the first line of his letter, James calls himself an apostle sent from Jerusalem.

cards.text: He calls himself “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” and then, straight out of the gate, no “how's the family,” James goes right to trials of many kinds.

cards.question: When his brothers run into trials of many kinds, what does James tell them to consider it?

cards.text: Pure JOY in trials? Friend, when my oven runs hot and the whole batch is on the line, joy is NOT my first word. But James gives a reason, about what the testing of their faith does.

cards.question: James says they can count trials as joy, because they know the testing of their faith develops ___.

cards.text: Then James says let perseverance finish its work, so don't yank the batch out early. I've done it, friend, and it's gooey in the middle EVERY time.

cards.question: When perseverance finishes its work, what does James say his brothers will be?

cards.text: Next, James talks to anyone who lacks wisdom. I once stood in front of an oven for ten minutes waiting on a batch, and the oven was OFF, so yeah, he's talking to me.

cards.question: According to James, anyone who lacks wisdom should ask ___.
James says God gives wisdom generously, but finds fault with whoever asks for it.

cards.text: But here's the catch: James says ask in faith, without doubting. Then he paints a picture of the person who doubts.

cards.question: What does James picture the person who doubts as?

answers.text: A wave tossed by the wind
A sheep lost from the flock
A lamp hidden under a bowl

cards.question: James says the person who asks while doubting should still expect to receive something from the Lord.

cards.text: James calls him a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways. That's me at the topping shelf going chocolate chips, no, sprinkles, no, WAIT, chocolate chips.
Next, James says the brother in humble circumstances should exult in his high position. The guy with the LEAST gets told he's sitting high? Friend, I like where this is going.

cards.question: If the humble brother exults in his high position, what does James say the one who is rich should exult in?
James says the rich man will pass away like a ___ of the field.

cards.text: The sun rises with scorching heat, and the flower falls and its beauty is lost. So too, James says, the rich man will fade away in the midst of his pursuits.
Then James circles right back to trials: blessed is the man who perseveres under trial.

cards.question: What does James say the man who perseveres under trial will receive once he has stood the test?
James says God has promised the crown of life to those who love Him.

cards.text: A CROWN, friend. I've got a tall white chef's hat, and I thought THAT was fancy. Then James turns to what someone should say when they're tempted.

cards.question: James says that when you're tempted, it's fine to say, “God is tempting me.”

cards.text: Not a chance. James says God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone.

cards.question: If God tempts no one, where does James say each person's temptation comes from?

cards.text: Lured away and enticed by his own desires, and nobody DRAGGED me to the chocolate chips either; I hopped over there, gold base and all. Then James says desire conceives and gives birth to sin.

cards.question: James traces it like a family line: desire gives birth to sin, and full-grown sin gives birth to ___.

cards.text: Then James says, “Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers.” BELOVED! The man who opened with one word of hello is getting soft on us.

cards.question: Where does James say every good and perfect gift comes from?

cards.text: And with the Father of the heavenly lights, there's no change or shifting shadow. The dead batteries I shared that drawer with kept arguing over who had the most charge left, but with God there's nothing to argue about.

cards.question: James says God chose to give us birth through the law of Moses.

cards.text: It's through the word of truth, so that we'd be a kind of firstfruits of His creation. Friend, I once got picked out of a bin for a quarter, but God CHOSE to give us birth? That's a whole different shelf.

findings.problem: James first appears as only 'a man named James.' The card holds back who he is. He calls himself 'a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ' in the same verse, and the card skips that so card 2 can quiz it.

rule.text: The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The baker is asked whether James calls himself an apostle sent from Jerusalem before any card has said how James describes himself. The only earlier card calls him 'a man named James,' so the pick is pure luck. Card 3 then tells the answer after the question.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to guess the exact image in the line ('like a ___ of the field') with no setup about passing away or withering. 'Tree' is also something of the field that withers, so a baker could argue for it. This tests wording the baker hasn't seen, not meaning they can reason out.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The card says James 'turns to what someone should say when they're tempted.' James 1:13 only gives what no one should say ('God is tempting me'). It never gives anything someone should say.

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The fact's core action is that the Father never changes or shifts. The comparison is batteries arguing over who has the most charge, which is about arguing, not changing. 'With God there's nothing to argue about' doesn't connect to 'no change or shifting shadow,' so the joke doesn't click.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: No earlier card sets up verse 18 or how God gives us birth. The baker has to guess whether it's 'the law of Moses' with nothing to reason from, and card 18 then tells the answer after the question.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.
